title: The five vowels never change
rule: a = ah · e = eh · i = ee · o = oh · u = oo — always, and every one of them is said
hook: English vowels are chaos: the a in cat, car, cake and about are four different sounds. Italian has five vowels and they only ever make one sound each. Nothing is silent — a final -e is always said out loud. Once you know the five, you can read any Italian word aloud, even one you've never met.

examples.hint: every vowel gets its turn: gra-tsi-e

examples.prompt: Now read it cold: Voglio andare a Roma
examples.hint: gl = ly, and every final vowel is pronounced

title: c and g change with the next letter
rule: before e or i: c = "ch", g = "j" · before a, o, u: c = "k", g = hard "g" · an h in between keeps it hard
hook: This one rule explains ciao, cappuccino, gelato and spaghetti all at once. The vowel after the c or g decides everything. And the h has no sound of its own — its whole job is to block the softening, which is why it's there in chi and spaghetti.

examples.hint: the h blocks the softening — hard g
the h means hard k, and é takes the stress

title: gn, gl and sc are single sounds
rule: gn = "ny" (onion) · gli = "ly" (million) · sc before e/i = "sh", elsewhere = "sk"
hook: Three letter pairs that don't behave like the letters in them. You already make all three sounds in English — in onion, million and shoe — you've just never spelled them this way.

examples.hint: gn = ny; and the ch keeps the k hard
the word for "the" (plural) — one sound, not g-l-i

title: Double letters are held twice as long
rule: a doubled consonant is one long sound, not two — and it changes the word
hook: In English, doubling is just spelling: dinner sounds like diner. In Italian it's real length, and it carries meaning. Hold the consonant, pause on it. Getting this wrong is the single most audible sign of an English accent.

examples.prompt: Which one is "grandfather": nono or nonno?
examples.hint: nono = ninth. The long n is the whole difference.

examples.prompt: Which one is "pen": pena or penna?

examples.hint: hold the f, and the stress is on the end
ano means something else entirely — hold the n!

examples.prompt: Now say both: capelli (hair) and cappelli (hats)
examples.hint: the doubled p is the only difference

title: Stress is usually second-to-last — and an accent tells you when it isn't
rule: default: stress the second-to-last syllable · an accent (à è ì ò ù) means stress the very last one
hook: Italian doesn't mark stress most of the time because it doesn't need to: it falls on the second-to-last syllable by default. When a word breaks that rule by landing on the final syllable, it must wear an accent — that's what the accent is for.

examples.hint: the accent drags it to the end

examples.prompt: So how do you say: università

title: -tion → -zione
rule: English -tion  →  Italian -zione (and it's always feminine: la … )
hook: Here's your first thousand words. Almost every English word ending in -tion exists in Italian with -zione on the end instead. They came from the same Latin word; English softened the t to a "sh" sound, Italian turned it into a "ts". Say -TSYOH-neh.

title: -ty → -tà
rule: English -ty  →  Italian -tà, with the stress crashing onto that final à
hook: Another few hundred words for free. Every -ty abstract noun becomes -tà. They're all feminine, and because the accent is on the end they never change in the plural — una città, due città.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "the city is beautiful"
examples.hint: the (feminine) = la · is = è · beautiful = bella

title: -ly → -mente
hook: How you turn a describing word into a how-you-do-it word. English glues -ly on the end; Italian glues -mente on the end. Same job, same position, so you can convert on the fly.

examples.hint: also what Italians shout when you finally arrive

title: -ble → -bile
hook: The "can be done" ending. English clipped the vowel out of it; Italian kept it. Put the -i- back and you have the Italian word.

title: -ous → -oso
hook: The "full of" ending — famous, nervous, curious. Swap -ous for -oso and you're there. If you're describing a woman or a feminine noun, it becomes -osa.

examples.hint: the soft c becomes z, as in -zione

title: -ate verbs → -are
rule: English verbs ending -ate  →  Italian -are (the plain "to …" form)
hook: -are is Italian's biggest verb ending, and English -ate verbs walk straight into it. The -are form is the dictionary form — the one that follows voglio, posso, devo.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I want to celebrate"

title: -ize / -ise → -izzare
hook: The other free verb ending. Everything you can -ize in English, you can -izzare in Italian — and modern words keep pouring into this one, so it keeps paying out.

examples.hint: the Greek y becomes an i — see the y → i bridge

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I have to organize it"
examples.hint: I have to = Devo · "it" (lo) hooks onto the end of the verb, and the -e drops

title: ct / pt → tt
hook: Italian doesn't like two different consonants clattering together — it makes them match. The c or p melts into the t and you get a doubled t. Once you hear it you'll spot it everywhere: perfetto, otto, settembre.

examples.hint: the x becomes s — Italian has no x

title: ph → f
hook: Italian simply spells the sound it hears. English keeps the Greek ph out of respect for the ancestors; Italian doesn't bother. Read ph as f and the word appears.

examples.hint: and the stress goes back: te-LE-fo-no

examples.prompt: Now build it — "where is the pharmacy?"

title: th → t
hook: Italian has no "th" sound at all. In the shared Greek and Latin words, the h just falls away and a plain t is left.

examples.prompt: Now say it — "the theatre is closed"

title: Greek y → i
rule: an English y in the middle of a word  →  Italian i
hook: English keeps the Greek y as a badge of origin. Italian writes what it says: i. This one usually travels with ph → f and th → t, because they're all in the same family of words.

examples.hint: ph → f and -ical → -ico all at once

examples.prompt: Now build it — "it's a typical problem"
examples.hint: problema is also masculine: un problema

title: -ist → -ista, -ism → -ismo
hook: A matched pair: the believer and the belief. Note -ista stays -ista for a man too — un artista, una artista — one of the few -a words that go either way.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I am a tourist"

title: -ance → -anza, -ence → -enza
hook: Same shift as -tion: that c sound hardens into a z. All of them are feminine.

examples.hint: ti → zi as well — you'll hear "pazienza!" ten times a day

examples.prompt: Now build it — "I don't have patience"

title: -ant / -ent → -ante / -ente
hook: Just add the vowel back on the end. These work as adjectives and as nouns, and they don't change between masculine and feminine — one less thing to think about.

examples.hint: the a in the first syllable becomes i

title: -ive → -ivo
hook: Straight swap. Watch how often it stacks with ct → tt — active, attractive, effective all double up their t on the way over.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "he is very positive"

title: -ic / -ical → -ico
hook: One ending covers both English forms. The stress lands two syllables from the end, which is unusual enough that it's worth saying aloud: eco-NO-mi-co… no — e-co-NO-mi-co.

title: -ary → -ario, -ory → -orio
hook: Two more endings that just want their vowel back.

title: -ure → -ura
hook: Small ending, but it covers some of the most useful nouns there are.

examples.hint: and the doubled t appears here too
the adjective follows the noun in Italian

title: -or / -er (a person) → -ore
rule: English -or or -er naming a doer  →  Italian -ore
hook: The "someone who does it" ending. The feminine is -rice: attore → attrice, direttore → direttrice.

examples.prompt: Now build it — "my father is a doctor"
